design_detail: Literature review with a pooled analysis of individually described published cases (the authors call it a research synthesis and pooled analysis; Springer labels it a review). PubMed cross-referenced with OVID Medline and the first 1000 Google Scholar results were searched to 23 April 2020 for 'excited' or 'agitated' and 'delirium', English only. 168 individually described cases of 'excited delirium syndrome' (ExDS, 120) or 'agitated delirium' (AgDS, 48) from 61 case reports and case series were pooled into one database and compared, fatal against survived and ExDS against AgDS, with univariate chi-square or Fisher tests and unadjusted odds ratios. 19 group-data studies are listed (Table 4) but not analysed. The authors state that the included designs do not fit the criteria for a systematic review and that PRISMA was followed where possible; AMSTAR 2 is applied here by analogy because the paper is a structured search with a pooled quantitative analysis.
can_establish: How the English-language case literature up to April 2020 used the label 'excited delirium' compared with 'agitated delirium': which published cases received each label, with what reported outcome, first responder, use of force, drugs noted and mental illness.
cannot_establish: Whether restraint, or any type of force, causes death in agitated delirium; whether such a state can be fatal without restraint; how often either presentation is fatal; or the mechanism of death (asphyxia was never measured). The cases are a publication-selected set in which the label, the outcome and how fully restraint was recorded all depend on the kind of source (forensic series of deaths against clinical reports of survivors), analysed without adjustment and without allowing for several cases coming from one article.

sample.recruitment: No people were recruited: cases were abstracted from published English-language case reports and case series found by the search (forensic pathology, toxicology, emergency medicine, psychiatry and police-practice sources; Table 1 also includes a repository document, Daugherty 2012, and a newsletter item, Miller 1998). Seven articles contribute 79 of the 168 cases (47%): O'Halloran and Frank 2000 (20), Stratton et al. 2001 (18), O'Halloran and Lewman 1993 (11), Dyer et al. 2001 (8), Mash et al. 2000 (8), Wetli and Fishbain 1985 (7) and Scaggs et al. 2016 (7) (editors' count from Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: articles describing a case report or case series of ExDS or AgDS (individual cases), or group characteristics of ExDS or AgDS (group data). Excluded: non-English articles, review articles, editorials, book chapters, physician brochures and web pages; nonspecific, paediatric or anaesthesia-emergence delirium; geriatric or palliative care; agitation or delirium judged to be neither ExDS nor AgDS; studies of a drug for undifferentiated delirium (Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Counts: 1342 records screened, 320 excluded by type or language, 941 judged ineligible, 81 retained (61 with individual cases, 20 with group data, 19 used after one overlapping report was dropped). The label was coded from the article's own terminology (Methods, 4th paragraph); the authors' 2023 reply shows that some cases were included or labelled by the reviewers where the source used neither term.
sample.demographics: 161 of 168 men (95.8%); age 30 or under for 84 (50.0%), 31 to 40 for 60 (35.7%), 41 or over for 24 (14.3%); race unknown for 95 (56.6%), White 40, Black 23, other 10; law enforcement first on scene in 111 (66.1%), paramedics in 37 (22.0%), others in 20 (11.9%); at least one known mental illness in 42 (25.0%) (Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 2). Countries and years of the events are not tabulated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. One case (Murphy et al. 2012) was dropped because the same case is described in more detail in another included article (Table 1 footnote), and one of 20 group-data papers was dropped as overlapping (Table 4 footnote).
sample.selection_effects: Strong, and named by the authors in part: deaths are more likely to be published and better documented (Discussion, 7th paragraph), and the forensic literature uses 'excited delirium' and describes deaths while the clinical literature uses both terms and describes survivors (Introduction, 5th paragraph). The pooled set therefore ties the ExDS label, death and detailed descriptions of restraint together through the type of source. Seven source papers whose titles name a death during restraint or restraint-related asphyxia contribute 55 cases (33%; editors' count from Table 1 and the reference list): O'Halloran and Frank 2000 (20), Stratton et al. 2001 (18), O'Halloran and Lewman 1993 (11), Stratton et al. 1995 (2), Rayamane et al. 2015 (2), Morrison and Sadler 2001 (1) and Kunz et al. 2018 (1); one more names a delayed in-custody death (Kennedy and Savard 2017, 1 case). The published critique (de Boer et al., 2023) adds that one source contributed only its 18 fatal cases out of about 214 restrained cases, that 11 included papers used neither term, and that several sources were misread; the authors' reply accepts three citation errors and a Table 4 error and disputes the rest.

exposure.measurement: Coded by the review team from each case description, in categories that are not mutually exclusive. Use of force: none, unknown, 'manhandle' (any manual force without handcuffs or devices, from a single blow to choke holds, tackling and pinning with body weight), handcuff, hog or hobble tie, TASER, sedation, and other or unspecified (pepper spray, four-point restraints, blunt objects). Drugs: the paper's 'drug intoxication', meaning the drugs described in the case (none noted, unknown, cocaine, alcohol, marijuana, stimulants meaning amphetamines, PCP, 'bath salts' and ecstasy, and other or unspecified, which the Discussion says included opiates, mushrooms and LSD); whether toxicology was done, on what sample and with what result was not extracted. Mental health: none noted, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, other. Type of authority: the first to arrive, with paramedic coded when police and paramedics arrived together (Methods, 4th and 5th paragraphs). Data curation is credited to one author; no duplicate extraction is reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not extracted. No drug amounts or blood concentrations were recorded, and the type, duration, position and force of restraint, the site of any compression and the timing of collapse were missing from most source reports, as the authors state (Discussion, 7th and 8th paragraphs).
exposure.polysubstance: Drug categories overlap and each is compared with all cases without it; combinations were not analysed. Table 2 counts 21 cases with no drug noted and 2 with drugs unknown, so 145 of 168 had at least one drug described (the text gives 147); 61 of the 64 survivors had a drug noted.

comparison.controls: For the outcome analysis, the 64 published cases who survived; for the label analysis, the 48 cases labelled AgDS. Each force, drug or mental-health category is compared with all cases without it. Only three cases had no force recorded, two of them fatal.
comparison.matching: None. No multivariable model, no stratification by type of source, publication period or first responder, and no allowance for cases clustered within articles.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Body size, heart or other disease, hyperthermia, the duration and intensity of the struggle, position and compression during restraint, the time from restraint to collapse, blood drug concentrations, tolerance, and the medical care received were not extracted; the authors name several of these as missing from the case literature.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Survivors also had drugs noted (61 of 64); marijuana and 'other' drugs were relatively more frequent among survivors, cocaine among deaths.

outcomes.instruments: Death or survival as reported in the source; the ExDS or AgDS label as used in the source or, for some cases, as judged by the reviewers. No case definition was applied; neither label is in ICD-9, ICD-10 or DSM-5 (Introduction, 6th paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable: there is no validated definition of either presentation, which the authors say makes case descriptions unsystematic.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Fatal' is a death reported in the source. The ExDS label is analysed both as an outcome (Table 3) and as an exposure for death (Table 2, OR 9.9).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; about 24 univariate comparisons per outcome (Tables 2 and 3), each at p ≤ 0.05, with no confidence intervals.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None; label, force, drugs and outcome were abstracted from the same case text by the review team.

analysis.effect_sizes: Unadjusted odds ratios with p-values and no intervals (Tables 2 and 3). Editors' calculation of Woolf 95% intervals from the printed counts, treating the 168 cases as independent (the intervals are too narrow because cases cluster within articles): death with the ExDS label 9.9 (4.5 to 21.5); with manhandling 7.4 (3.6 to 15.4); handcuffs 10.7 (5.0 to 22.8); hog or hobble tie 50 (6.7 to 374); TASER 2.3 (0.7 to 7.4); sedation 0.04 (0.01 to 0.10); cocaine noted 2.7 (1.4 to 5.1); marijuana noted 0.10 (0.04 to 0.29); no drug noted 4.3 (1.2 to 15.1); paramedic rather than police first on scene 0.06 (0.03 to 0.16; printed as 0.3, reporting issue 1). ExDS rather than AgDS label with handcuffs 14 (5.5 to 35.7), manhandling 4.7 (2.2 to 10.1), hog or hobble tie 29.2 (3.9 to 219), sedation 0.09 (0.04 to 0.20).
analysis.covariates: None. Age was categorized because its relation was not linear (Results, 3rd paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Every coded variable appears in Tables 2 and 3. The group-data studies were tabulated but not analysed because only 8 of 19 described restraint. The case database and code are available on request only (Availability of data and material).
analysis.power: Not addressed. Several cells hold 0 or 1 case (one survivor and one AgDS case with a hog or hobble tie; no survivor and no AgDS case of 'other' race), so those odds ratios are very imprecise; only 3 cases without force exist, so the risk of death without restraint cannot be estimated from these data.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 168 published cases, the ExDS label went with death (92 of 120 ExDS-labelled cases died, against 12 of 48 AgDS-labelled cases), with police as first responders, and with handcuffs, hobble ties and manual force; the AgDS label went with survival, paramedics and sedation. Some force was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths, a count that includes sedation, TASER and 'other' categories; force was recorded as absent in 2 deaths and unknown in 8. Only 3 cases (2 fatal) had no force recorded. Cocaine was noted more often in deaths and marijuana in survivors. No adjusted analysis, no measure of asphyxia and no detail of restraint beyond its type were available.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that there is no evidence for ExDS as a cause of death without restraint and that, after aggressive restraint, restraint-related asphyxia "must be considered a likely cause of the death" (Abstract); the Discussion calls the findings strong evidence (1st paragraph) and recommends abandoning ExDS and recording the manner of death of restrained AgDS cases as homicide or undetermined (12th paragraph). Gaps: (1) the label-death and label-restraint associations are what the split between sources described in the authors' own Introduction would produce (forensic death series use ExDS and describe restraint; clinical reports of survivors use AgDS and describe sedation), and this was not analysed; (2) the absence of evidence for death without restraint reflects a case literature with almost no unrestrained cases (3, of whom 2 died), not evidence against such deaths; (3) asphyxia, position, duration and compression were never measured, so the mechanism is the authors' inference; (4) the fall in the fatal share over time (90% before 2000, 56% after) is not adjusted for the changing mix of sources; (5) the 79% mortality of the group-data ExDS studies, used to dispute a published fatality figure under 10%, came from a Table 4 the authors later corrected (about 64% with their corrected values; editors' arithmetic) and is set mainly by how many post-mortem series were included; (6) the illustrative per-use risk of death from methamphetamine draws its consumption figure from a web page (drugabuse.com, reference 95), gives no clear source for the roughly 2,700 deaths (reference 96, cited after the risk figure, is a federal report on drug-impaired driving), and is a population figure for any use, not the risk in a person already in severe agitated delirium. In the 2023 reply the authors describe a regression showing a monotonic rise in death with more aggressive restraint, and in 2024 say their results conclusively demonstrated the point; the paper reports only univariate comparisons of overlapping force categories, with no trend test. In the paper's favour, the Discussion lists the selection and information limitations plainly and says no reliable conclusion can be drawn about the two unrestrained deaths.

timeline.event: Wetli and Fishbain describe 'excited delirium' in seven deaths after cocaine use with no anatomical cause found at autopsy (as described in this paper's Introduction, 2nd paragraph).
Stratton et al., people restrained for excited delirium in paramedic care: about 214 restrained cases, 18 fatal, according to de Boer et al. (2023); this paper pooled only the 18 fatal cases.
American College of Emergency Physicians white paper presents ExDS as a distinct clinical entity (as described in this paper's Discussion, 10th paragraph).

Vilke et al. defining review, cited for an ExDS fatality under 10%, a figure this paper traces to an unrelated 2007 study of first-episode psychosis (Discussion, 5th paragraph; not read by the editors).
Gonin et al. systematic review of excited delirium (definitions, epidemiology, pathophysiology, management), on whose methods this paper's search built (not read in this round).
This pooled analysis of 168 published cases (search to 23 April 2020).

de Boer, Fronczek and Archer, commentary (10.1007/s12024-023-00589-3; PMC10752912, read): ExDS papers were mostly non-clinical and AgDS papers clinical, so the label-death association is confounded by source; several sources misread (Baldwin et al. 2016, 71 of 73 survived; Strote et al. 2014, no deaths; Stratton et al. 2001, survivors ignored); 16 sources selected on death; conclusions called misleading. No competing interests declared.

Freeman, Strömmer, Leith and Zeegers, reply (10.1007/s12024-023-00616-3; PMC10752838, read): accept three miscited sources (Byard, Penders, Schiavone) and a transcription error in Table 4, print a corrected Table 4 inside the reply (Baldwin 3% mortality, Strote 2014 0%, Strote 2006 28 cases), dispute the other points and say results and conclusions are unchanged. No correction notice is linked to the 2020 article on PMC or Springer.

de Boer et al., 'More on' letter (online December 2023; 10.1007/s12024-023-00722-2; PMC11525397, read): the reply shows labels were sometimes assigned by the reviewers without a stated definition; questions leaving out about 194 non-fatal restrained cases from one source; argues that cause of death in restrained delirious people is not a choice between ExDS and asphyxia.

Freeman et al., second reply (10.1007/s12024-023-00736-w; Springer HTML, read): restates the conclusions; declares that two authors provide medicolegal consultation, including in cases of death in custody.

Gonçalves Dias and Cainé, systematic review of deaths in custody, physical restraint, excited delirium and medico-legal investigation (not readable in this round: the publisher's site refused the browser).

replication.where_it_stands: Contested. This pooled analysis is the main quantitative argument that 'excited delirium' deaths are restraint deaths under another name. Its one published critique (two letters) disputes the extraction and the causal reading; the authors' replies accept a Table 4 error and three miscitations but not the critique's substance. Nobody has re-extracted the cases and re-run the analysis with source type and clustering by article in the model. The paper may be cited for how the ExDS label has been applied in published cases and for the near-absence of unrestrained cases in that literature, not for the cause of any death, for a fatality rate, or for the effect of any restraint type.

funding.funder: Not reported: neither the PMC full text nor the Springer article page carries a funding statement (open access, CC BY 4.0).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article has no conflict-of-interest statement. In the authors' second reply (2024, 10.1007/s12024-023-00736-w), Freeman and Strömmer declare that they provide medicolegal consultation services, including in cases of death in custody. The authors' 2023 reply (PMC10752838) carries no conflict-of-interest statement either.
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors at the CAPHRI School for Public Health and Primary Care, Maastricht University; by 2024 Freeman also held a chair of forensic and legal medicine at the Royal College of Physicians, London (second reply). The Discussion says the authors of the experimental restraint studies, some of whom also wrote the ACEP white paper, "manufactured an artificially low ExDS mortality rate" (6th paragraph). The critics (de Boer, Fronczek, Archer) declare no competing interests.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective registry, or a linkage of police use-of-force, ambulance, emergency-department and death-investigation records, covering every encounter with a person in agitated delirium, fatal or not, with one case definition applied without knowledge of the outcome, and recording restraint type, position, duration, number of officers and compression, sedation, blood drug concentrations and medical history, so that death can be analysed with adjustment for these and for setting. The authors propose such a registry (Discussion, 9th paragraph); re-extracting the published cases with source type and clustering by article in the model would be the near-term check.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: The two questions (whether restraint confounds the link between the ExDS label and death; whether ExDS differs from AgDS apart from death), the case population, the exposures (force types, drugs, mental illness, first responder), the comparators (survivors; AgDS) and the outcomes (death; label) are stated (Introduction, 7th and 8th paragraphs; Methods).

Case reports and series are included because they are the only literature describing individual cases; the authors say these designs do not fit a systematic review (Introduction, 6th paragraph; Methods, 1st paragraph).

PubMed cross-referenced with OVID Medline (one bibliographic database through two interfaces) and the first 1000 Google Scholar results, with search words and date given; English only without justification (item 4 as written); reviews excluded; no reference-list or citation searching, registries or contact with experts reported.

Not reported; data curation is credited to one author. The extraction errors later acknowledged (three miscited sources, Table 4 mortality) and disputed (labels assigned where sources used neither term) bear on this item.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons are given only as categories in the text and in the flowchart (Figure 1, an image); the 941 eligibility exclusions, which turned on whether a case counted as ExDS or AgDS, are not listed, and the stage at which they were made is not clear.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives only author, year and number of cases per article; no setting, label, outcome or force per source. Table 4 describes the group studies (source, restraint reporting, mortality), with errors later corrected. The case database is available on request only.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No appraisal of the completeness or quality of the source reports; missing detail is discussed only in general terms.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Cases from 61 articles were pooled as one sample and compared with univariate chi-square or Fisher tests: no allowance for clustering within articles (seven articles supply 47% of cases), no stratification by type of source or first responder, no adjustment, overlapping exposure categories each compared with all other cases, and no intervals.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Limitations of the case literature are listed (Discussion, 7th to 9th paragraphs), but how they would bias the main comparison is not examined, the authors argue that the limitations cut both ways, and the conclusions are stated as strong evidence.
The difference between forensic death series and clinical reports is described in the Introduction but not investigated as a source of heterogeneity in the pooled comparisons.

The authors note that deaths are over-represented in the published literature but do not examine how this reporting bias affects the comparisons; formal small-study tests do not apply to case reports, but an analysis stratified by type of source would have.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding or conflict-of-interest statement in the article (PMC and Springer pages) or in the 2023 reply; a declaration of medicolegal consultation by two authors appears only in the 2024 reply.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 was built for reviews of intervention studies; it is applied here by analogy because the paper is a structured search with a pooled quantitative analysis of published cases. Seven critical items are not met (2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15), which gives critically low confidence in the pooled comparisons as a summary of the evidence. Beyond the checklist, the main problem is confounding by source: the label, the outcome and how fully restraint was recorded all depend on whether a case came from a forensic death series or a clinical report, and the analysis neither stratifies by source nor allows for 47% of the cases coming from seven articles; the extraction itself is disputed in a published critique, and the authors have corrected one table only inside a reply. The card may be cited for how the ExDS and AgDS labels were applied in the published case literature up to April 2020, for the near-absence of cases without recorded force (3 of 168), and for the authors' position and recommendations on certification, labelled as theirs. It may not be cited for the risk of death with or without restraint, for any restraint type causing death, for asphyxia as the mechanism, for a fatality rate of either presentation, or for cocaine, marijuana or any other drug raising or lowering the risk of death.

key_findings.finding: How a case and a death entered the pooled data: an individually described case of ExDS or AgDS in an English-language case report or series found by the search; 'fatal' means the source reported a death. Neither label has an ICD code. The label is the source authors' own term (forensic pathologists, emergency physicians and others), coded by the reviewers from the article's terminology. Drugs are those described in the case (the paper's 'drug intoxication'): no toxicology results, concentrations, or share of cases tested were extracted. The comparisons are the 64 published survivors and the 48 AgDS-labelled cases.
key_findings.note: The authors' 2023 reply (PMC10752838) states that some cases were included or labelled by the reviewers where the source used neither term (for example two cases of GHB withdrawal coded as AgDS), which the Methods do not describe.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: PubMed cross-referenced with OVID Medline (445 records) and the first 1000 Google Scholar results, to 23 April 2020; 1342 records screened after removing duplicates; 320 excluded as non-English, reviews, editorials, chapters, brochures or web pages; 941 judged ineligible (delirium not called ExDS or AgDS, or no case described); 81 retained: 61 articles with 168 individual cases (Table 1) and 20 group-data papers (19 used).
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Cases: 161 of 168 men (95.8%); race unknown in 95 (56.6%); law enforcement first on scene in 111 (66.1%); at least one known mental illness in 42 (25.0%); the text gives some drug intoxication in 147 (86.3%) and some use of force in 138 (81.5%).
key_findings.note: The two percentages fit 145 and 137 cases, which is what Table 2 gives (168 minus 21 with no drug noted and 2 unknown; 168 minus 3 with no force and 28 unknown); see reporting issue 3.

key_findings.finding: 104 of 168 cases (61.9%) were fatal: 92 of 120 ExDS-labelled cases (76.7%) and 12 of 48 AgDS-labelled cases (25.0%); unadjusted odds ratio 9.9, p < 0.0001 (editors' Woolf 95% interval 4.5 to 21.5, treating cases as independent).
key_findings.locator: Results › Analysis of outcome; Results › Analysis of diagnosis; Tables 2 and 3, Diagnosis and Outcome death rows

key_findings.finding: Use of force in fatal (n = 104) against survived (n = 64) cases: manhandling 68 (65.4%) against 13 (20.3%), OR 7.4; handcuffs 74 (71.2%) against 12 (18.8%), OR 10.7; hog or hobble tie 46 (44.2%) against 1 (1.6%), OR 50; TASER 14 (13.5%) against 4 (6.3%), OR 2.3, p = 0.14; sedation 6 (5.8%) against 40 (62.5%), OR 0.04; other or unspecified 44 (42.3%) against 22 (34.4%), OR 1.4, p = 0.31; force unknown 8 (7.7%) against 20 (31.3%); no force 2 (1.9%) against 1 (1.6%). Categories overlap; odds ratios unadjusted, without intervals.
key_findings.locator: Results › Analysis of outcome; Table 2, Use of force rows

key_findings.finding: Some form of force was recorded in 94 of the 104 deaths (90%), a count that includes sedation, TASER and 'other' (pepper spray, four-point restraint, blunt objects) as well as physical restraint; force was recorded as absent in 2 deaths (2%) and unknown in 8 (8%). Among the 64 survivors, 43 (67%) had some force recorded, 1 none and 20 (31%) unknown. The authors say no reliable conclusion can be drawn about the cause of the 2 deaths without described restraint.
key_findings.locator: Results › Analysis of outcome; Discussion, 1st and 12th paragraphs; Table 2
key_findings.note: The Results give 68% for survivors with restraint; the counts give 43 of 64 (67.2%), as the Discussion says.

key_findings.finding: ExDS-labelled (n = 120) against AgDS-labelled (n = 48) cases: police first on scene 95 (79.2%) against 16 (33.3%); manhandling 70 (58.3%) against 11 (22.9%), OR 4.7; handcuffs 80 (66.7%) against 6 (12.5%), OR 14; hog or hobble tie 46 (38.3%) against 1 (2.1%), OR 29.2; sedation 16 (13.3%) against 30 (62.5%), OR 0.09; other or unspecified force 39 (32.5%) against 27 (56.3%), OR 0.4; mental illness other than schizophrenia or bipolar disorder 9 (7.5%) against 13 (27.1%), OR 0.2.

Drugs noted in fatal against survived cases (presence as described in the source report, not toxicology results): cocaine 55 (52.9%) against 19 (29.7%), OR 2.7, p = 0.003; alcohol 16 (15.4%) against 6 (9.4%), OR 1.8, p = 0.26; marijuana 5 (4.8%) against 21 (32.8%), OR 0.1, p < 0.0001; stimulants (amphetamines, PCP, 'bath salts', ecstasy) 28 (26.9%) against 24 (37.5%), OR 0.6, p = 0.15; other or unspecified 18 (17.3%) against 24 (37.5%), OR 0.4, p = 0.003; no drug noted 18 (17.3%) against 3 (4.7%), OR 4.3, p = 0.02.
key_findings.locator: Results › Analysis of outcome; Table 2, Drug intoxication rows
key_findings.note: The authors explain these differences through the kind of force each drug state attracted (Discussion, 2nd paragraph), citing Figure 2 (restraint type by drug), an image that could not be viewed; no adjusted analysis was done, so the drug associations are not estimates of any drug's effect on death.

key_findings.finding: ExDS-labelled cases more often had cocaine noted (60, 50.0%, against 14, 29.2%; OR 2.4, p = 0.01), alcohol (20, 16.7%, against 2, 4.2%; p = 0.03) or no drug noted (19, 15.8%, against 2, 4.2%; p = 0.04); AgDS-labelled cases more often had marijuana (12, 25.0%, against 14, 11.7%; p = 0.03) or other drugs (25, 52.1%, against 17, 14.2%; p < 0.0001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Analysis of diagnosis; Table 3, Drug intoxication rows

key_findings.finding: Of the 30 cases published before 2000, 90% were fatal; of the 138 published from 2000 to 2020, 56% were fatal. The authors attribute the fall to growing awareness of restraint asphyxia; no test, and no adjustment for the type of source, is reported.
key_findings.note: Consistent with Table 1 (30 cases in articles dated before 2000) and with 27 + 77 = 104 deaths (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Group-data studies as published: of 19, 4 used AgDS (153 cases, 5 deaths, 3%) and 15 used ExDS (666 cases, 529 deaths, 79%); 10 drew on post-mortem sources, 7 on hospital data and 2 on police data; the studies with low or no mortality were hospital studies and one police study; only 8 of 19 described restraint, so no conclusion on restraint was drawn from them.
key_findings.locator: Results › Analysis of group data studies; Table 4
key_findings.note: Table 4 was corrected in the authors' 2023 reply (PMC10752838, Appendix Table 1): Baldwin (73 cases) 3% rather than 100% mortality, Strote 2014 (43 cases) 0% rather than 100%, Strote 2006 28 cases rather than 3. With those values the 15 ExDS studies give about 440 deaths in 691 cases (64%; editors' arithmetic). The 79% in the Results and Discussion was not corrected.

key_findings.finding: The authors report that a published ExDS fatality of under 10% (Vilke et al. 2012) and one of 8.3% (the 2009 ACEP white paper) both cite a 2007 study of substance use in first-episode psychosis that, on their reading, contains no mortality figure and uses 8.3 only as a standard deviation of IQ.
key_findings.note: The editors have not read the papers concerned; this is the authors' account.

key_findings.finding: Background stated by the authors, citing others: no autopsy finding identifies ExDS, and drug levels in body fluids in these deaths are typically in the recreational rather than the fatal range, so the diagnosis is one of exclusion; neither ExDS nor AgDS is listed in ICD-9, ICD-10 or DSM-5.
key_findings.note: Second-hand statements (references 6, 7, 14 and 20 of the paper), not results of this analysis.

key_findings.finding: Recommendations for death investigation: abandon 'excited delirium syndrome' in favour of 'agitated delirium' with a modifier for the presence and degree of restraint; record the manner of death of fatal AgDS cases with restraint as homicide or undetermined, not natural or accident; investigate such deaths with a full autopsy, toxicology and a detailed account of the type and duration of restraint and force.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 and the text give the odds of death for paramedics first on scene as 0.3 and for 'other' responders as 0.06, relative to police; the printed counts (paramedic 7 died and 30 survived; other 10 and 10; police 87 and 24) give 0.06 for paramedics and 0.28 for others (editors' calculation), so the two values are swapped.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Analysis of outcome; Table 2, Type of authority rows
reporting_issues.consequence: The paramedic contrast is about five times stronger than printed; the direction is unchanged. It strengthens the case that the first responder (and the type of source) is tied to outcome, which the analysis did not adjust for.

reporting_issues.issue: The race odds ratios do not match their rows. Table 2: Black against White is printed 1.4, but the counts (12 and 11 against 22 and 18) give 0.89; 'other' (10 deaths, no survivors) cannot have a finite odds ratio but is printed 0.9; 'unknown' is printed >999.9 but its counts give 1.4. Table 3: 'other' is printed 0.4 and 'unknown' >999.9, but the counts give no finite value for 'other' (no AgDS case) and 0.45 for 'unknown'. Table 3 also prints 14.7% for 17 of 120 Black ExDS cases (14.2%) and 8.1% for 10 of 120 'other' (8.3%).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Tables 2 and 3, Race rows
reporting_issues.consequence: Race was not significant either way, but these and the authority values show that odds ratios in the tables were misplaced; every value used in a claim should be recomputed from the counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give drug intoxication in 147 cases (86.3%) and use of force in 138 (81.5%); 147/168 is 87.5% and 138/168 is 82.1%. Table 2 counts give 145 with a drug described (86.3%) and 137 with force recorded (81.5%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; use the counts from Table 2 (145 and 137).

reporting_issues.issue: The share of survivors with some restraint is 68% in the Results and 67% in the Discussion; Table 2 gives 43 of 64 (67.2%).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Analysis of outcome; Discussion, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that mortality associated with an ExDS diagnosis was 62% among the individual cases, but 62% (104 of 168) is the fatal share of all ExDS and AgDS cases together; Table 3 gives 92 of 120 (76.7%) for ExDS.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 5th paragraph; Tables 2 and 3
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison the Discussion draws with published fatality figures uses the wrong individual-case number; 76.7% is the ExDS figure, and neither figure is a fatality rate because the cases are publication-selected.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the most aggressive forms of restraint raised the odds of an ExDS diagnosis by 7 to 29 times; Table 3 gives 4.7 (manhandling), 14 (handcuffs) and 29.2 (hog or hobble tie). The 7 appears to be the odds ratio for death with manhandling (7.4, Table 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: The lower bound of the stated range is overstated, and 'increased the odds' describes an unadjusted association as an effect.

reporting_issues.issue: Key points, item 3, says only 2% of fatalities lacked a description of some form of restraint; Table 2 gives 2 deaths with no force and 8 with force unknown, so 10 of 104 (9.6%) had no restraint described.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Key points, item 3; Table 2, Use of force rows
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary overstates how completely restraint is documented in the fatal cases.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 lists Baldwin et al. (2016) with 73 ExDS cases and 100% mortality from police data, although the paper's own reference 1 is titled as a study of non-fatal use-of-force encounters; the authors' 2023 reply corrects this (3%) together with Strote 2014 (0% rather than 100%), Strote 2006 (28 cases rather than 3) and Cole 2018 (emergency department rather than inpatient). The correction is printed only inside the reply; no correction notice is linked to the article on PMC or Springer, and the 79% (529 of 666) in the Results and Discussion stands uncorrected.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 4; Results › Analysis of group data studies; Discussion, 5th paragraph; reference 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The 79% group-data mortality for ExDS should not be cited; with the authors' corrected values it is about 64% (editors' arithmetic), and in either version it mainly reflects how many post-mortem series were included.

reporting_issues.issue: Age groups are described as 30 or under, 30 to 40 and over 40 in the Results, but the tables label them less than 30, 31 to 40 and 41 or over.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 3rd paragraph; Tables 2 and 3, Age rows
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the group a 30-year-old falls into is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the label was coded from the article's terminology, but the authors' 2023 reply shows cases taken from sources that used neither term and labelled by the reviewers (for example two GHB-withdrawal cases coded AgDS), and accepts that three Table 1 sources were miscited (Byard, Penders, Schiavone; the reply gives the intended references).
reporting_issues.consequence: The label, which is both outcome and exposure in the analysis, partly reflects the reviewers' judgment rather than the source authors' usage, and Table 1 cannot be used as printed to audit the cases.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives p = 0.003 for 'other or unspecified' force by label; Table 3 gives 0.004.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Analysis of diagnosis; Table 3

reporting_issues.issue: Discussion, 1st paragraph describes the 'other or unspecified' force category as less aggressive forms of restraint (pepper spray, four-point restraint), but the Methods define it as also including blunt objects; the Discussion's statement that AgDS was 2.5 times more likely to be diagnosed with these forms is the inverse of Table 3's odds ratio of 0.4.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 1st paragraph; Methods, 4th paragraph; Table 3, Use of force rows
reporting_issues.consequence: The category mixes pepper spray and four-point restraint with blunt objects, so its association with the AgDS label cannot be read as an association with milder force.

reporting_issues.issue: Results › Analysis of outcome says the frequency of drug use differed significantly for most categories and lists alcohol (more common in deaths) and stimulants (more common in survivors) with cocaine, marijuana and other drugs, but Table 2 gives p = 0.26 for alcohol and 0.15 for stimulants. The Discussion (2nd paragraph) says the marijuana and 'other' drug associations with survival held regardless of diagnosis, but no analysis stratified by label is reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Analysis of outcome; Table 2, Drug intoxication rows; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The alcohol and stimulant differences are not statistically supported, and the statement that the drug associations hold whatever the label has no analysis behind it.
